01 / Project overview

One plan, from first idea
to everyone’s response.

The product helps an organizer decide what to do, where to meet, who to invite and when to go. Invitees can understand the plan and respond, while summary and calendar views keep upcoming activities in sight.

CONTRIBUTION

End-to-end product design

Competitive exploration, organizer and invitee flows, wireframes, mobile and desktop UI, and shared component patterns.

SCOPE

A connected experience

Onboarding, recurring availability, contacts, immediate and future plans, polls, invitation review, RSVP states and event views.

EVIDENCE

Design artifacts, not launch claims

The supplied file contains research references and both platform designs. Dates, team size, release status and business metrics were not supplied.

02 / The problem statement

Making plans shouldn’t
be the hard part.

How might we make casual plans easier to agree on without turning a meetup with friends into a formal appointment?

01. Different levels of certainty

Sometimes the plan is “right now.” Sometimes there is a date. Sometimes the group needs to choose. One rigid scheduling path cannot express all three intentions clearly.

02. Decisions without context

An invitee needs the activity, place, time and people involved before deciding. Those details should travel with the invitation.

03. An unclear next step

After a response or vote, the interface must make the result and available follow-up actions visible.

Evidence label: this problem framing is synthesized from the supplied design flows. It is not presented as a finding from interviews or observed customer behavior.

03 / People & needs

Two sides of the same plan.

Role-based proto-personas help make the organizer and invitee needs explicit.

HYPOTHESES · NOT RESEARCH PARTICIPANTS
AJ
Fictional persona · Organizer

Alex, the plan starter

Coordinates a group

Alex has an activity in mind and wants to turn it into a clear invitation without managing every response separately.

Primary goal
Get a plan agreed and make the next step obvious to everyone.
Likely friction to validate
Uncertain availability, repeated coordination and friends who are not already using the product.
Design response
Now / Later / Poll, a review step, public-link invitations, and visible response counts.
Testable question
Can organizers choose the right timing mode and send an invitation without assistance?
SL
Fictional persona · Invitee

Sam, the flexible joiner

Decides on the go

Sam receives a plan and needs enough information to decide quickly, with a way to express uncertainty or vote on timing.

Primary goal
Understand the invitation and respond with confidence.
Likely friction to validate
Missing context, uncertainty about available times and doubt about whether a response was recorded.
Design response
Activity, place and time together; Yes / No / Maybe states; voting and confirmation.
Testable question
Can invitees explain the plan, submit a response and recognize the confirmation?

No invented demographics, interview quotes or sample sizes are attached to these personas. Validate them through research before treating them as representative user segments.

04 / Research & discovery

Familiar scheduling.
A more social tone.

Six products appear in the original reference collection. The analysis below combines that documented review with a separate check of official product documentation on 14 October 2026.

Visuals above are schematic pattern sketches, not competitor screenshots. The implications are design judgments; they are not usability scores.

What this changes in the design: combine recognizable scheduling and response patterns with casual language. Polls are an established pattern in several competitors; they are not claimed as a unique invention or a proven market gap.
Research provenance and limitations

The Figma notes explicitly describe Google Calendar’s familiar event creation and calendar views, Partiful’s casual tone and attendance visibility, and Calendly’s clean but formal presentation. Doodle, Eventbrite and Evite appear as reference collections. No interview transcripts, survey datasets, task-test results or scored competitive audit were found.

The official-source check is an additional desk-research pass for this HTML edition, not evidence that those sources informed the original project.

05 / Process & exploration

Let the intention
choose the flow.

The wireframes branch around timing while preserving the same planning model. The flows below are reconstructed from the screen sequence, not a claim of a tested “before and after.”

Meet now

Activity + place
Choose invitees
Select Now
Review → Send invitation

Meet later

Activity + place
Choose invitees
Choose time + duration
Review → Send invitation

Poll the group

Activity + place
Choose candidate times
Review → Share poll
Invitees vote → Confirmation
Invitee journey
Open invitation → Review details → Respond or vote → Recognize confirmation → Update when needed

Wireframes made the structure tangible.

Speed / flexibility

Separate immediate plans from later plans and polls. The benefit is a focused path; the cost is an initial choice that must be understood.

Overview / density

Summary cards support scanning; calendar views support time planning. Multiple views require consistent labels and states.

Reach / setup effort

Public links and text invites address friends outside the product. Availability and contact setup need a clear purpose and a skip path.

These trade-offs are inferred from the design alternatives. The original decision-meeting record was not supplied.

06 / Final solution

One language.
Two planning surfaces.

Mobile concentrates on quick decisions; desktop gives the same ideas more room. Explore anonymized copies of the supplied screens.

DESIGN INTENT

Keep the next step visible.

A clear review action, named timing modes and recognizable event details connect creation with the invitation experience.

Screen copies preserve the supplied layouts. Figtree substitutes unavailable fonts, and identities and brand marks are anonymized.

07 / Design system & components

A system you can explore.

Warm, clear, consistent.

The palette is drawn from the supplied color variables. The HTML component kit below reinterprets the existing buttons, fields, cards and response controls.

New documentation and demo states are additions for this case study. They have not been published as shared Figma library components.

  • Typeface in design: Figtree. HTML uses a local system sans-serif fallback to work offline.
  • Proposed spacing scale: 4 / 8 / 12 / 16 / 24 / 32 / 48.
  • Proposed radii: 12 px fields, 18–24 px cards, full-round buttons.
  • Demo interaction: visible keyboard focus, explicit labels and inline error text.
  • Motion: subtle transitions; reduced-motion preference respected.

Contrast references and component guidance

Ratios are calculated from opaque color pairs. They do not validate gradients, images, transparency or every original screen. Normal text needs 4.5:1; large text and applicable non-text controls need 3:1. Inactive controls and logo text have applicable contrast exemptions. These checks do not establish full WCAG compliance.

09 / Impact & results

What the work demonstrates.
What still needs measuring.

2Platforms represented in the source designs
3Planning modes: Now, Later and Poll
6Competitor reference collections

The artifacts demonstrate connected organizer and invitee journeys. They do not prove increased conversion, revenue, retention or faster task completion. No launch analytics or validated before-and-after results were supplied.

Proposed measurement plan · not achieved results
QuestionMeasureValidation approach
Do people complete onboarding?Completed setup ÷ onboarding startsMeasure step-level exits; separate optional skips from failures.
Can organizers create a plan?Invitations sent ÷ creation startsInstrument creation, review and send with consistent event definitions.
How much effort does it take?Median time to first invitationReport abandonment and error rates alongside duration.
Do invitees respond?Responses or votes ÷ unique invitation opensSegment Now / Later / Poll and mobile / desktop.
Is the flow understandable?Unassisted task completionTest organizer and invitee tasks; report sample size and observed errors.

Reflection

Keep one recognizable planning model, then adapt its density to the device.

Next validation priorities

Check whether people understand the timing modes, feel comfortable with the phone and contact steps, and can recognize a successful response. Test keyboard access, screen-reader behavior and real-device layouts before shipping.

The personas and new HTML interactions remain hypotheses and prototypes. They are not evidence of research or implementation completed during the original project.
